newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil Senate approves torture bill amid outrage.
newsitem.headline: Brazil Senate approves torture bill amid outrage.

text.p: Brazil's Senate approved on Thursday a bill that classifies torture as a crime for the first time, three days after the country's latest human rights outrage involving police.
The upper house of Congress approved unanimously the bill which is expected to be signed into law by President Fernando Henrique Cardoso, an official said.

The legislation languished in the Senate for six months but was rushed to the top of the agenda after a television station on Monday showed video footage of police officers allegedly beating up and extorting money from civilians, allegedly killing one.
The images caused widespread revulsion in Brazil and sparked instant protests from international human rights groups.
According to a poll released on Thursday, fear and mistrust of the police rose sharply in Sao Paulo after the videotape was aired.

The Folha de Sao Paulo daily, which published the survey, said the number of people who said they feared the military police more than they trusted them rose to 74 percent from around 50 percent in a similar poll conducted in December 1995.
That figure dropped sharply among those who had not seen the videotape. Of those, 54 percent said they mistrusted the police while 44 percent felt safe.
The poll showed mistrust of the police was especially high among blacks -- 83 percent said they lived in fear of the police -- and people who had been stopped for identity checks.
The survey questioned 1,080 people in an unspecified period of time and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points.

The bill approved on Thursday punishes torture with jail sentences of between two and eight years, rising to 16 years in fatal cases. Currently, police and military officers accused of mistreatment of civilians and prisoners are punishable for the lesser crime of battery.

"This bill fills a vacuum in Brazilian law and represents a big step forward in our campaign for the respect of human rights," said Senator Ramez Tebet, who was in charge of the legislation in the Senate.
